---
title: "Statistical analysis cookbook"
subtitle: "Map the clinical question and study design to a defensible R workflow."
---

::: {.callout-important}
This is a starting map, not an automatic test selector. Independence, pairing, clustering, outcome distributions, causal aims, missingness and the estimand may require a different method.
:::

## Choose a starting method

| Clinical question | Outcome/design | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Does one mean differ from a reference? | Continuous, one sample | `t.test(x, mu = reference)` |
| Do two independent groups differ? | Continuous | `t.test(outcome ~ group, data = data)` |
| Did the same patients change? | Paired continuous measurements | `t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE)` |
| Do more than two groups differ? | Continuous | `aov(outcome ~ group, data = data)` |
| Are two categorical variables associated? | Counts | `chisq.test(table(x, y))` |
| Are two continuous variables associated? | Continuous pair | `cor.test(x, y)` |
| How does a continuous outcome vary? | Continuous outcome | `lm()` |
| How does event probability vary? | Binary outcome | `glm(..., family = binomial())` |

## Two independent groups

```r
two_group_result <- t.test(
  outcome_score ~ treatment,
  data = analysis_data
)

tidy(two_group_result, conf.int = TRUE)
```

Report group summaries, the estimated difference, confidence interval, p-value, assumptions and clinical importance. Welch’s t-test is the default in R and does not assume equal group variances.

## Paired measurements

```r
paired_result <- t.test(
  analysis_data$followup_score,
  analysis_data$baseline_score,
  paired = TRUE
)
```

Pairing requires correct row alignment: each baseline value must correspond to the same person’s follow-up value. The analysis concerns within-person differences.

## More than two groups

```r
anova_model <- aov(outcome_score ~ treatment_group, data = analysis_data)
summary(anova_model)
TukeyHSD(anova_model)
```

The global ANOVA asks whether all population means are equal. Post-hoc or planned comparisons estimate which contrasts differ while accounting for multiplicity.

## Categorical association

```r
outcome_table <- table(
  analysis_data$treatment,
  analysis_data$outcome
)

chi_result <- chisq.test(outcome_table)
chi_result
chi_result$expected
```

Inspect observed and expected counts and ensure observations are independent. Sparse expected cells may require an exact or alternative method.

## Correlation

```r
correlation_result <- cor.test(
  analysis_data$exposure,
  analysis_data$outcome,
  method = "pearson"
)
```

Visualise the relationship first. Pearson estimates linear association; Spearman estimates monotonic ranked association. Neither establishes causation.

## Linear regression

```r
linear_model <- lm(
  outcome_score ~ treatment + age_years + baseline_score,
  data = analysis_data
)

tidy(linear_model, conf.int = TRUE)
plot(linear_model)
```

Interpret each coefficient using its units and reference group. Diagnostics concern linearity, residual patterns, influence, independence and the fitted model—not a ritual pass/fail checklist.

## Logistic regression

```r
logistic_model <- glm(
  adverse_event ~ treatment + age_years + baseline_severity,
  data = analysis_data,
  family = binomial()
)

tidy(logistic_model, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

With `exponentiate = TRUE`, coefficients are presented as odds ratios. Confirm which event is coded as 1 and retain “odds” in the interpretation.

## A complete analysis sequence

1. State the clinical question and estimand.
2. Prepare and count the analysis population.
3. Describe outcome and groups visually and numerically.
4. Run the prespecified method and store its result.
5. Examine assumptions and influential observations.
6. Extract the effect estimate and uncertainty.
7. Perform justified sensitivity analyses.
8. Translate the result into clinical language.
9. State limitations and what the analysis cannot show.
